title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
author: Malcolm X (with Alex Haley)
citation: Malcolm X, and Alex Haley. The Autobiography of Malcolm X. Grove Press, 1965.

sections.heading: Excerpts: Chapters 1, 2, 11, and 19

epigraph.quote: Education is the passport to the future, for tomorrow belongs to those who prepare for it today.

paragraphs: When my mother was pregnant with me, she told me later, a party of hooded Ku Klux Klan riders galloped up to our home in Omaha, Nebraska, one night. Surrounding the house, brandishing shotguns and rifles, they shouted for my father to come out. My mother opened the front door, standing straight and tall in the light, and told them that she was alone with her small children and that my father was away preaching in Milwaukee.

My father, the Reverend Earl Little, was an itinerant Baptist preacher and an organizer for Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Garvey's philosophy of Black self-reliance, economic independence, and pride in African heritage captivated my father. But it enraged the local white supremacists. Two of my father's brothers had already been lynched in Georgia, and another was shot to death by police.

When I was six years old, after we had moved to Lansing, Michigan, our home was set on fire in the dead of winter by members of the Black Legion, a local white vigilante group. I remember being awakened by smoke and sparks falling onto my bed. We rushed out into the snow in our nightclothes and stood watching our home burn to ashes while the white police and firemen stood by, refusing to lift a hand.

Two years later, my father was murdered. His body was found laid out across the municipal streetcar tracks, his skull crushed and his body cut almost in two. The white coroner ruled it a suicide or accident, so the insurance company refused to pay my mother the life insurance policy he had faithfully maintained. My mother struggled to feed eight children during the Great Depression, taking in laundry and scrubbing floors until the county welfare workers drove her to a breakdown and separated us into foster homes.

At Mason High School, I was at the top of my class. I was elected class president in the eighth grade. But one day, my English teacher, Mr. Ostrowski, asked me what career I wanted to pursue. When I told him proudly that I wanted to become a lawyer, he leaned back, looked at me with pity, and said: 'Malcolm, one of life's first needs is for us to be realistic. A lawyer—that's no realistic goal for a nigger. You've got to think about something you can do. Why not become a carpenter? People like you, and you're good with your hands.'

That was the turning point of my youth. I realized that no matter how intelligent, ambitious, or diligent a Black person was in America, white society saw him only through the lens of racial subservience. Soon afterward, I dropped out of school and went to Boston, and later Harlem, plunging into the underworld of numbers running, narcotics, and burglaries.

In prison at Charlestown and Norfolk, my true education began. My brother Reginald introduced me to the teachings of Elijah Muhammad and the Nation of Islam. I obtained a dictionary from the prison library and copied every single word and definition by hand into notebooks, from A to Z, expanding my vocabulary until I could read history, philosophy, and sociology under the glow of the corridor nightlight.

My pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964 completed my transformation. There, kneeling beside Muslims of every complexion—blonde-eyed, dark-skinned, blue-eyed Europeans, Africans, and Asians—I realized that the brotherhood of man was possible when people recognized the oneness of humanity under God. In my final years, I fought not for separation, but for human rights, declaring that freedom, justice, and equality must be attained by any means necessary.
